lessons.title: How the Great Lakes Were Made
lessons.mainIdea: Ice sheets a kilometer thick scraped out the Great Lakes basins and flattened Illinois, then melted back about 14,000 years ago.
reading: Stand on the lakefront in Chicago and look north across water that stretches to the horizon. Lake Michigan is about 500 kilometers long and in places 280 meters deep. No river could dig that. The lakes are the work of ice. During the last *ice age*, the Laurentide ice sheet spread from Canada across the northern United States. At its greatest extent, about 20,000 years ago, ice more than a kilometer thick covered most of Illinois.

A glacier is a slow bulldozer. Its weight and motion pluck rock from the ground and drag it along. The ice sheet followed old river valleys in soft rock and gouged them deeper and wider into the basins of the Great Lakes. When it reached harder rock, it scraped and polished it. The ground-up rock, from boulders to flour-fine clay, was carried south and dumped in a blanket geologists call *glacial till*. The flat, deep, fertile soil of central Illinois is mostly this till, topped by windblown dust from the dried-out glacial floodplains.

The ice began to melt back about 18,000 years ago. Where its edge paused, it left ridges of rubble called *moraines*; the low hills that curve around Chicago's suburbs are moraines. Meltwater filled the basins in front of the retreating ice. An early, larger version of Lake Michigan, which geologists call Lake Chicago, stood higher than today's lake and drained south through the Illinois River valley. Its old shorelines still show up as low ridges in the city. By about 14,000 years ago most of Illinois was ice-free, and the lakes have settled into their present shapes over the thousands of years since.

The evidence is everywhere once you know to look. Granite boulders lie in Illinois fields, hundreds of kilometers from any granite bedrock, carried down from Canada. Grooves scratched by rock in the ice mark exposed bedrock. Layers of till stack up from more than one glacial advance. The Great Lakes are young by Earth's standards, a few thousand years old in their current form, and still slowly changing as the land, freed of the ice's weight, rises a few millimeters a year.

words.d: a long cold period when ice sheets cover large parts of the continents
the unsorted mix of clay, sand, gravel and boulders dropped by a melting glacier
a ridge of rock and soil piled up at the edge of a glacier
a glacier large enough to cover a whole region or continent

look.title: A Geologist Reads the Boulders
look.text: In his 1840 book on glaciers, the Swiss scientist Louis Agassiz argued that the scattered boulders, polished bedrock and scratched surfaces found far from any mountains across northern Europe could not have been left by floods, and were instead the marks of vast sheets of ice that had once covered the land and later melted away.
look.cite: Louis Agassiz, Études sur les glaciers (Studies on Glaciers), 1840
look.prompt: Before Agassiz, many people explained scattered boulders with a great flood. What could a glacier do that a flood could not, and how would the evidence differ?

check.q: Where did the granite boulders in Illinois farm fields come from?
choices: Ancient Illinois volcanoes
Carried from Canada by the ice sheet
Deposited by the Mississippi River
Meteorites
check.why: Illinois has no granite bedrock. The boulders were plucked from the Canadian Shield and dragged south by the glacier.

check.q: What are the low hills curving around Chicago's suburbs?
choices: Old sand dunes
Folded rock from a plate collision
Moraines left where the ice edge paused
Piles of river sediment
check.why: As the ice sheet melted back, it dropped rubble at each pause in its retreat, forming curved ridges called moraines.

check.q: Why is central Illinois so flat and fertile?
choices: It was never touched by glaciers
It was the bottom of the ocean until recently
Volcanic ash built up its soil
Glaciers spread a thick blanket of ground-up rock over the old landscape
check.why: Glacial till and windblown dust buried the older hills and valleys under deep, mineral-rich soil.

review.q: What problem kept most geologists from accepting Wegener's idea in the 1920s?
choices: He could not explain what force moved the continents
The continents do not actually fit together
No fossils matched across the Atlantic
He had never seen a map
review.why: Wegener's evidence was strong, but his proposed mechanisms were wrong, and critics used that to reject the whole idea.

review.q: Which discovery in the 1960s confirmed that ocean floor spreads from the ridges?
choices: Coal under Antarctica
Mirrored magnetic stripes on both sides of the mid-ocean ridge
The New Madrid earthquakes
Glacial scratches in India
review.why: Vine and Matthews found symmetric stripes recording magnetic reversals, exactly as seafloor spreading predicted.

review.q: Which observation shows Earth's outer core is liquid?
choices: Lava is liquid
The crust floats
S waves do not pass through it
The core is hot
review.why: S waves need a solid. Their shadow zone on the far side of Earth revealed a liquid layer.

review.q: What drives the slow motion of the mantle?
choices: Ocean tides
The sun's heat
Wind
Heat from Earth's formation and radioactive decay causing convection
review.why: Internal heat makes deep rock rise and cool rock sink, a convection that carries the plates.

review.q: A cave forms as slightly acidic rainwater dissolves rock. Which rock is it most likely dissolving?
choices: Limestone
Granite
Basalt
Slate
review.why: Limestone, made of calcium carbonate, dissolves in weak acid. Illinois and Kentucky caves are cut in it.

review.q: Why do ice cores show carbon dioxide and temperature rising and falling together over the past 800,000 years?
choices: Because scientists adjusted the data
Because carbon dioxide traps heat and warming releases more carbon dioxide from the oceans, a feedback
Because ice cores cannot measure gases
Because volcanoes erupt more in warm periods
review.why: Orbital cycles start the change; carbon dioxide feedback amplifies it. The two records move together in the cores.

review.q: What did John Tyndall measure in 1859?
choices: The age of the Earth
The speed of plate motion
Which gases absorb heat radiation
The temperature of the core
review.why: Tyndall showed that carbon dioxide, methane and water vapor absorb heat radiation while nitrogen and oxygen do not.

review.q: Lake Chicago, the early form of Lake Michigan, drained to the south. What does that tell you?
choices: The lake was smaller than today
The lake was salty
Illinois was under the ocean
Ice still blocked the northern outlets, so meltwater escaped through the Illinois River valley
review.why: With the ice sheet still to the north, the only way out was south, which is why old shorelines and outlet valleys run that way.

chapters.title: Human Sustainability
chapters.bigQuestion: How can people use Earth's resources and live with its hazards without using up what the next generation needs?

story.title: The Day the Prairie Came to Washington
story.kicker: Farmers plowed up the grass that held the Great Plains together, and when the rain stopped, the soil itself took to the air.
paragraphs: For thousands of years a thick mat of grass roots held the soil of the southern Great Plains in place through droughts and wind. In the 1910s and 1920s, high wheat prices and new tractors changed that. Farmers in the panhandles of Oklahoma and Texas, and in Kansas, Colorado and New Mexico, tore up millions of acres of grassland and planted wheat. In wet years it paid. Then, starting in 1931, the rain stopped.

Wheat withered and the bare, powdery soil lay open to the wind. The storms began in 1932 and grew. On April 14, 1935, a day remembered as Black Sunday, a wall of dust more than a kilometer high rolled across the plains, turning afternoon to midnight. People lost their way a few meters from their doors. Dust drifted like snow against fences and buried farm machinery. Children and old people sickened with dust pneumonia. Hundreds of thousands of families packed up and left.

A year earlier, in May 1934, one storm had lifted dust so high that the wind carried it east across the whole country. It dimmed the sky over Chicago, then over Washington and New York, and settled on the decks of ships in the Atlantic. In Washington, a soil scientist named Hugh Hammond Bennett had been warning for years that the nation was throwing away its soil. Now the soil had come to the capital to make his argument for him. By many accounts he timed a Senate hearing in the spring of 1935 so that senators could look out the window at the haze while he spoke.

Congress passed the Soil Conservation Act in April 1935, and Bennett led the new Soil Conservation Service. Its agents taught farmers to plow along the contour of hills, to plant rows of trees as windbreaks, to rotate crops and to leave stubble on the field. The rains returned in 1939, and when drought came again in the 1950s, the land held far better. The Dust Bowl was not a natural disaster alone. It was drought plus decisions, and different decisions changed the outcome.
story.think: The farmers who plowed the plains were not foolish; wheat paid and the rain seemed reliable. What information, if they had it, might have changed their choices?

lessons.title: Renewable or Not
lessons.mainIdea: A resource is sustainable only if people use it no faster than nature replaces it; some resources are replaced in years, some never.
reading: Everything people build, eat and burn comes from Earth. A *natural resource* is anything from the planet that people use: water, soil, wood, fish, coal, copper, sunlight. The useful question is not whether a resource is big but how fast it comes back. A *renewable resource* is replaced by natural processes about as fast as it is used, like sunlight, wind, and a forest cut no faster than it regrows. A *nonrenewable resource* forms so slowly that for human purposes it is a fixed stock: oil, coal, natural gas, metal ores.

The line is not always sharp. Soil is renewable, but slowly: it can take centuries for natural processes to build a few centimeters of topsoil, and a single dust storm or hard rain can strip that away. Groundwater in some aquifers refills every year; in others it has been sitting since the ice age and refills so slowly it is effectively nonrenewable. A fishery is renewable until fishing outruns breeding, and then it collapses. Renewable means renewable at a rate.

Illinois sits on some of the largest coal deposits in the United States. Coal formed here from swamp forests about 300 million years ago and will not form again on any timescale that matters to people. It powered the state's industry for over a century. Today most of Illinois's coal-burning power plants have closed or are scheduled to, because natural gas, wind and nuclear power cost less and because of the pollution coal produces. The coal is still in the ground; the decision about whether to burn it is a human one.

*Sustainability* means meeting today's needs without wrecking the ability of the future to meet its own. The test is simple to state and hard to do. Use renewable resources no faster than they renew. Use nonrenewable ones while building replacements. Do not release waste faster than Earth's systems can absorb it. Every lesson in this chapter is a case of that test being passed or failed.

words.d: anything from Earth that people use, such as water, soil, minerals or fuel
a resource replaced by natural processes about as fast as it is used
a resource that forms so slowly it is a fixed supply for human purposes
meeting present needs without destroying the ability of future people to meet theirs

look.title: Where U.S. Energy Came From in 2022
look.prompt: What share of U.S. energy came from nonrenewable sources? Which slice would you expect to change fastest over the next twenty years, and why?

check.q: Which best describes a renewable resource?
choices: One that is replaced by natural processes about as fast as it is used
One that is very large
One that is free
One that never runs out no matter how it is used
check.why: Renewable means renewable at a rate. Even forests and fish can be used up if harvest outpaces regrowth.

check.q: Why is topsoil treated as a nonrenewable resource by many farmers even though it does form naturally?
choices: Because soil is made of rock
Because it forms over centuries but can be lost in a single storm
Because it cannot be moved
Because plants do not need it
check.why: The rate of formation is so slow compared with the rate of possible loss that, in practice, lost soil is gone for generations.

check.q: Illinois coal is still in the ground, but most coal power plants in the state are closing. What does this show?
choices: The coal has been used up
Coal is now a renewable resource
Whether a resource gets used depends on cost, alternatives and pollution, not only on how much exists
Illinois no longer needs electricity
check.why: Resource decisions weigh price, cleaner options and health costs. A large supply does not by itself mean it will be used.

lessons.title: Water Under the Prairie
lessons.mainIdea: Groundwater is a shared, slowly refilled store; pumping faster than recharge draws it down for everyone.
reading: Dig a well in central Illinois and you may reach water that fell as rain thousands of years ago. Beneath the soil lie layers of sand and gravel left by glaciers, and their pores are full of water. A layer that holds enough water to pump is an *aquifer*. The Mahomet Aquifer, buried in an ancient river valley across central Illinois, supplies drinking water to hundreds of thousands of people and irrigates farms. Wells share it; a pump in one town lowers the water in the next.

Water enters an aquifer by *recharge*: rain and snowmelt soaking down through soil and rock, which can take years to decades. If people pump faster than recharge, the *water table*, the level below which the ground is saturated, drops. Wells go dry, shallowest first. Rivers and wetlands fed by groundwater shrink. In the High Plains west of Illinois, the Ogallala Aquifer has been pumped for irrigation for decades faster than it refills, and in parts of Kansas and Texas the water level has fallen tens of meters.

Chicago and its suburbs face the opposite geography: a vast lake next door. But use of Lake Michigan water is limited by a U.S. Supreme Court decree, because the water Illinois takes and sends down the Illinois River is water that leaves the Great Lakes for good. Suburbs beyond the pipes once relied on deep sandstone aquifers that dropped hundreds of feet over the twentieth century, and several have since switched to lake water or river water instead.

Groundwater is invisible, which makes it easy to overuse. You cannot see the water table fall the way you can watch a reservoir shrink. Managing it takes measurement: monitoring wells, records of pumping, and models of how the aquifer responds. Illinois's state surveys have tracked the Mahomet and the sandstone aquifers for decades. Data, not guesswork, tells a town whether its water will still be there in fifty years.

words.d: an underground layer of sand, gravel or porous rock that holds enough water to pump
water soaking down from the surface to refill an aquifer
the level underground below which the soil and rock are saturated with water

look.title: Three Wells on One Aquifer
look.text: A farm, a bottling plant and a small town each drill a well into the same sand-and-gravel aquifer. The town's monitoring well has recorded the water level every month for thirty years. For the first twenty years the level rose in wet springs and fell in dry summers, ending each year about where it began. In the last ten years, since the plant opened, each year ends about half a meter lower than the last.
look.prompt: What does the monitoring record show about pumping versus recharge, and who is affected first if the trend continues?

check.q: What happens when an aquifer is pumped faster than it is recharged?
choices: The water table stays the same
The water table drops and the shallowest wells fail first
The aquifer fills with rock
Recharge speeds up to match
check.why: Storage falls when withdrawal exceeds inflow. Shallow wells are the first to go dry as the water table sinks.

check.q: Why is Illinois's use of Lake Michigan water limited by a court decree?
choices: The lake is too polluted to drink
Lake water is too cold for pipes
Water sent down the Illinois River leaves the Great Lakes for good and other states share the lakes
Chicago has its own aquifer
check.why: Diversion out of the Great Lakes basin lowers a resource shared by several states and Canada, so the amount is capped.

check.q: Why is groundwater especially easy to overuse compared with a reservoir?
choices: Groundwater is free
Groundwater refills instantly
Groundwater cannot be measured
You cannot see the water level fall without monitoring wells and records
check.why: An underground store gives no visible warning. Only measurement reveals a falling water table before wells fail.

lessons.title: Powering Illinois
lessons.mainIdea: Every energy source has costs and benefits; Illinois's mix of nuclear, gas, wind, solar and coal reflects a series of trade-offs.
reading: Flip a switch in Illinois and the electricity most likely came from a nuclear plant. Illinois has more nuclear reactors than any other state, and they supply roughly half of the electricity generated here. A reactor splits uranium atoms to boil water and spin turbines. It releases no carbon dioxide while running, and one plant can power millions of homes. The trade-offs are real too: plants are expensive to build, the used fuel stays radioactive for thousands of years and still has no permanent national storage site, and accidents, though rare, can be severe.

Coal built the state's grid in the twentieth century. It still supplies some power, but its share has fallen sharply. Burning coal releases more carbon dioxide per unit of electricity than any other common fuel. It also releases sulfur, mercury and fine particles that damage lungs. Natural gas burns cleaner and can ramp up quickly when demand spikes. But it still emits carbon dioxide, and leaks of methane, a strong greenhouse gas, add to its climate cost.

The prairie has become an energy field. Illinois ranks among the leading wind-power states, with rows of turbines across the flat farmland of the central counties, and solar farms are spreading. Wind and sun cost nothing as fuel and emit nothing in operation. Their weakness is timing: the wind drops and the sun sets, so a grid built on them needs storage, long transmission lines, or backup power. Turbines and panels also take land, though farming can continue between turbines.

No source wins on every count. Engineers and lawmakers compare them on cost, reliability, land use, water use, air pollution, greenhouse gases, waste and safety. A 2021 Illinois law set a schedule to phase out carbon emissions from the state's power plants over the coming decades while supporting workers in coal towns. Whether that schedule is met depends on the same things this lesson lists: technology, price and choices.

words.d: electricity made by using the heat from splitting uranium atoms to boil water and drive turbines
a set of blades spun by wind, water or steam to turn a generator
the network of power plants, lines and transformers that delivers electricity
the main gas in natural gas; a strong greenhouse gas when it leaks

look.title: Roosevelt on Conserving Resources, 1907
look.text: In his annual message to Congress in December 1907, President Theodore Roosevelt told lawmakers that conserving the nation's natural resources and using them wisely was the fundamental problem beneath almost every other problem of national life, and he warned that the country was using up its forests, soils and minerals as if the supply were endless.
look.cite: Theodore Roosevelt, Seventh Annual Message to Congress, 1907
look.prompt: Roosevelt was writing about forests and minerals. Does his argument apply to energy choices today, and what has changed since 1907?

check.q: What is the main advantage of nuclear power for the climate?
choices: It uses no water
It produces no waste
It emits no carbon dioxide while operating
It is the cheapest plant to build
check.why: Fission releases heat without burning carbon. The drawbacks are cost, long-lived waste and accident risk, not emissions.

check.q: What is the main weakness of wind and solar power for a grid?
choices: They emit methane
They use uranium
They cost more in fuel than coal
Their output depends on weather and time of day
check.why: Fuel is free and operation is clean, but supply varies. Storage, transmission or backup power is needed to match demand.

check.q: Why has coal's share of Illinois electricity fallen?
choices: Cheaper alternatives, health costs of pollution and climate rules made it less attractive
The coal ran out
Coal plants need too much land
Coal cannot make steam
check.why: Gas, wind and nuclear cost less per unit, and coal's sulfur, particles and carbon dioxide carry health and regulatory costs.

lessons.title: Hazard, Exposure and Risk
lessons.mainIdea: Risk depends on the hazard, on who and what is in its path, and on how well they can withstand it; people can change the last two.
reading: An earthquake in an empty desert is a hazard but not a disaster. The same earthquake under a city of unbraced brick buildings is a catastrophe. Scientists separate the pieces. A *natural hazard* is the physical event: the shaking, the flood, the tornado, the heat. *Exposure* is who and what sits in its path. *Vulnerability* is how badly those people and structures would be hurt. *Risk* is all three combined. People rarely control the hazard, but they can change exposure and vulnerability, and that is where most lives are saved.

Consider the New Madrid seismic zone. In the winter of 1811 to 1812 it produced some of the strongest earthquakes in the recorded history of the eastern United States. Few people lived there, so few died. Today the same zone lies near St. Louis, Memphis and southern Illinois, with millions of people, old brick buildings, bridges, pipelines and the Mississippi's levees. The hazard is roughly what it was. The exposure has grown enormously. Building codes in the region now require quake-resistant design for new construction, which reduces vulnerability.

Measuring the hazard is the first step. Seismographs map where quakes cluster and how often. Stream gauges and rainfall records let hydrologists estimate the *hundred-year flood*, the flood level with a 1 percent chance in any given year, a term many people misread as once a century. Doppler radar tracks the rotation inside storms. From these records come maps, and from maps come decisions: where to build, how to build, and what to insure.

Risk also carries values that science alone cannot settle. How safe is safe enough? Who pays to retrofit a school? A town may accept a small flood risk to keep a river view, or decide that a rare but terrible outcome is worth expensive protection. Science can say how likely and how bad. Communities decide what to do about it.

words.d: a natural event that can cause harm, such as an earthquake, flood or tornado
the people, buildings and systems located where a hazard can reach them
how much harm a hazard would do to the people and structures it reaches
the chance of harm, combining hazard, exposure and vulnerability
a flood level with a 1 percent chance of occurring in any single year

look.title: Same Storm, Two Towns
look.text: Two river towns the same size face the same spring flood crest. Town A has kept its floodplain as parks and ball fields, requires new houses to sit above the hundred-year flood line, and drills an evacuation plan each April. Town B built a subdivision on the floodplain behind an old levee that has never been inspected. The crest arrives at 2 a.m.
look.prompt: The hazard is identical. Break down how exposure and vulnerability differ, and what each town could still change before next spring.

check.q: A magnitude 6 earthquake strikes an empty desert; an identical one strikes a city of brick buildings. What differs?
choices: The hazard
The magnitude
The type of fault
The exposure and vulnerability
check.why: The physical hazard is the same. Who is in its path and how well their buildings hold up determine the risk and the outcome.

check.q: What does a hundred-year flood mean?
choices: A flood with about a 1 percent chance of happening in any given year
A flood that happens exactly once every century
The largest flood that can ever occur
A flood that lasts a hundred days
check.why: It is a probability per year, not a schedule. Two such floods can happen in back-to-back years.

check.q: Why is the New Madrid zone a bigger risk today than in 1812, even though the hazard is about the same?
choices: Earthquakes have grown stronger
Far more people and structures now lie in the zone
The Mississippi has moved
Building codes have been abolished
check.why: Exposure has grown from a few settlers to millions of people and critical infrastructure. Risk rises with exposure even when the hazard does not.

lessons.title: Too Much Water, Too Little
lessons.mainIdea: Floods and droughts are natural, but levees, paving, drainage and land use change how much damage they do.
reading: In the summer of 1993 rain fell on the upper Midwest for weeks. The Mississippi and Missouri rivers rose past every mark on their gauges. Levees, the earthen walls built to hold rivers in their channels, failed one after another. Water covered towns from Iowa to Missouri, closed the river to barges for weeks and flooded farmland across Illinois. It was among the most costly floods in United States history. The rain was extraordinary, but the damage was not only about rain.

A river naturally spreads onto its *floodplain* in high water, slowing and dropping sediment. *Levees* keep the water in the channel, which protects the land behind them but pushes the water higher and faster downstream, toward the next town's levee. Cities make it worse by paving. Rain that once soaked into prairie sod now races off roofs and parking lots into storm drains. Chicago answered its own flooding with the Deep Tunnel, begun in 1975: enormous tunnels and reservoirs carved in rock beneath the city to hold storm water until treatment plants can catch up.

Drought is the quieter hazard. In 2012 much of Illinois went weeks without meaningful rain during the hottest part of the growing season, and corn yields fell sharply. Drought does not knock down houses, but it drains reservoirs, stresses aquifers, kills crops and sets the stage for fire. On the Great Plains in the 1930s, drought plus bare soil made the Dust Bowl. The hazard was drought; the vulnerability was plowed land with nothing holding it.

The responses are a mix of engineering and restraint. Engineering: levees, reservoirs, tunnels, improved forecasts from the National Weather Service. Restraint: keeping buildings off floodplains, restoring wetlands that soak up water, planting cover crops that hold soil and moisture. After 1993, some Illinois and Missouri river towns took federal buyouts and moved to higher ground rather than rebuild in the same place. That is a choice to reduce exposure instead of fighting the hazard.

words.d: the flat land beside a river that naturally floods in high water
a wall of earth or concrete built along a river to keep flood water out
a long period with much less rain than usual
rain that flows over the surface instead of soaking into the ground

look.title: USGS on the 1993 Flood
look.text: In its report on the 1993 flood, the U.S. Geological Survey described record-high river levels at many gauging stations on the Mississippi and Missouri rivers, noted that the flooding lasted for weeks across a large part of the Midwest, and reported that many levees were overtopped or failed, inundating farmland and towns in several states.
look.cite: U.S. Geological Survey, report on the 1993 Midwest floods, 1993
look.prompt: Levees protected some towns and failed at others. Why might building a taller levee on one bank raise the risk for a town across the river or downstream?

check.q: How does paving a city change the way rain behaves?
choices: More rain soaks into the ground
Rain runs off faster into drains and rivers, raising flood peaks
Rain evaporates before hitting the ground
Paving prevents flooding
check.why: Prairie soil absorbs rain slowly. Roofs and pavement shed it instantly, so streams and sewers get a sharp surge.

check.q: What is one downside of levees?
choices: They make rivers dry up
They push flood water higher and faster onto places downstream
They cause droughts
They cannot be built on the Mississippi
check.why: A levee keeps water off one floodplain, so the river has less room to spread and rises higher for the next stretch.

check.q: After 1993, some towns accepted buyouts and moved to higher ground. Which part of risk did that change?
choices: The hazard
The rainfall
The river's speed
The exposure
check.why: The river will still flood. Moving people and buildings out of its path removes them from harm, reducing exposure.

lessons.title: Heat and Violent Storms
lessons.mainIdea: Warnings, shelter and social connection decide whether heat waves and tornadoes become tragedies.
reading: In July 1995 a dome of hot, humid air settled over Chicago for five days. Temperatures topped 40 degrees Celsius, and nights stayed hot enough that bodies never cooled. More than 700 people died, most of them elderly, poor and living alone in upper-floor apartments without air conditioning, some with windows nailed shut out of fear of crime. Heat is the deadliest weather hazard in the United States in many years, and it kills quietly, one person at a time.

The 1995 disaster showed that vulnerability is social as much as physical. Neighborhoods with the same heat had very different death tolls. Where people knew their neighbors and checked on them, more survived. Chicago now opens cooling centers, sends workers door to door during heat emergencies, and issues warnings days ahead. Cities are also hotter than the countryside because pavement and roofs absorb sunlight, an *urban heat island* that adds several degrees on the worst days. Trees and reflective roofs cut it.

Illinois also sits in the path of the strongest thunderstorms on Earth. When warm, moist air from the Gulf of Mexico meets cold, dry air from the north, storms can rotate and spawn a *tornado*. The deadliest tornado in United States history was the Tri-State Tornado of March 18, 1925. It ran for more than three hours across Missouri, Illinois and Indiana. It killed nearly 700 people, most of them in southern Illinois. There were no warnings at all; the word tornado was not even used in forecasts then.

Today Doppler radar can see rotation inside a storm before a funnel touches down, and the National Weather Service issues warnings that reach phones within seconds. Average warning time is now many minutes rather than zero. That does not stop the tornado. It changes vulnerability: time to reach a basement or an interior room. Building codes that anchor roofs and add safe rooms in schools do the same. The hazard has not shrunk since 1925; the death toll from a comparable storm would.

words.d: several days of unusually hot weather, often dangerous when nights stay hot
the extra warmth of a city caused by pavement and roofs absorbing sunlight
a violently rotating column of air reaching from a thunderstorm to the ground

look.title: Two Apartment Buildings, One Heat Wave
look.text: Two brick apartment buildings stand a block apart in Chicago during a five-day heat wave. In the first, a tenant council keeps a list of every older resident and knocks on each door every afternoon, and the lobby is kept cool with a rented air conditioner. In the second, residents mostly do not know one another, and the elevator is broken. Both buildings reach the same indoor temperature.
look.prompt: The hazard is identical. What makes one building more vulnerable, and which changes cost almost nothing?

check.q: Why did the 1995 Chicago heat wave kill so many people who lived alone?
choices: Living alone raises body temperature
Nobody checked on them, and social isolation increased their vulnerability
Their apartments were on the ground floor
They lived outside the heat island
check.why: The same heat hit everyone. People with neighbors who checked on them were far more likely to be found and helped.

check.q: What makes a city hotter than the surrounding farmland on the same day?
choices: Cities have more people breathing
Farms are closer to the ocean
Pavement and roofs absorb and store sunlight
Cities get more direct sun
check.why: Dark, dry surfaces soak up solar energy and release it slowly, while plants and soil cool the air by evaporation.

check.q: Doppler radar and phone alerts do not change the tornado itself. What do they change?
choices: The hazard
The exposure of buildings
The wind speed
The vulnerability of people, by giving them time to shelter
check.why: Warning time lets people reach a safe place. The storm is the same; its ability to hurt people is reduced.

lessons.title: From Prairie to Cornfield
lessons.mainIdea: Converting nearly all of Illinois's prairie to farmland fed millions and also removed the deep roots that built and held the soil.
reading: Two hundred years ago, tallgrass prairie covered more than half of Illinois, grasses taller than a person with roots reaching 3 meters down. Those roots built some of the richest soil on Earth, black and deep. Then the steel plow, invented by John Deere in Illinois in 1837, made it possible to cut the dense sod. Within a few decades the prairie was corn and wheat. Today less than one percent of the original prairie remains, in scattered patches along old railroad lines and in cemeteries.

The change was a huge human success by one measure. Illinois farmland now produces more corn and soybeans than almost any place on the planet and feeds people and livestock around the world. By another measure it opened a slow leak. Row crops leave soil bare for half the year. Rain and wind carry it off. Across the Corn Belt, topsoil has been lost at rates far faster than it forms, and in places the dark layer is noticeably thinner than it was a century ago.

*Erosion* is the same process that ate the Great Plains in the 1930s, only slower and wetter. It also carries fertilizer and soil into streams. The prairie had another job: its roots and the wetlands scattered across it held rain and released it slowly. Drained and tiled fields send water straight to ditches and rivers, adding to the flood peaks in the previous lesson. One change in land use touches soil, water and hazards at once.

Farmers and scientists have answers, many of them borrowed from the Soil Conservation Service. *No-till* farming leaves last year's stalks in place and plants through them, so the soil is never bare. *Cover crops* such as rye grow through winter and hold the ground. Strips of restored prairie along field edges catch runoff. These practices cost money and time up front and pay back over years, which is the central tension of sustainability.

words.d: the grassland of tall grasses and wildflowers that once covered much of Illinois
the loss of soil as water or wind carries it away
farming that plants seeds through the previous crop's residue instead of plowing
a crop such as rye grown between main crops to protect and hold the soil

look.title: Roosevelt on the Drought, 1936
look.text: In a radio address in September 1936, after touring the drought-stricken Plains, President Franklin Roosevelt described farm families he had met whose crops and water had failed, and he argued that the nation's task was not only to relieve their suffering but to change how the land was used, through soil conservation, water storage and tree planting, so that future droughts would do less harm.
look.cite: Franklin D. Roosevelt, fireside chat on drought conditions, September 6, 1936
look.prompt: Roosevelt separated relief from prevention. Which of the practices he named change the hazard, and which change vulnerability?

check.q: What did prairie roots do that a cornfield does not?
choices: Hold soil and rain year-round with deep, permanent roots
Produce more grain
Prevent all flooding
Add carbon dioxide to the air
check.why: Prairie plants keep living roots in the ground all year. Annual crops leave bare soil for months and shallow roots the rest of the time.

check.q: How does no-till farming reduce erosion?
choices: It removes all plants from the field
It leaves crop residue covering the soil so rain and wind cannot strip it
It floods the field
It plows deeper
check.why: Cover on the surface breaks the force of raindrops and wind, so far less soil moves.

check.q: Why do many farmers hesitate to adopt cover crops even though they protect soil?
choices: Cover crops make soil worse
Cover crops are illegal in Illinois
They cost money and effort now while the benefits arrive slowly over years
Cover crops attract tornadoes
check.why: Sustainability often trades a present cost for a future benefit, and that trade is hard when budgets are tight.

lessons.title: What Flows Downstream
lessons.mainIdea: Fertilizer and waste from Illinois travel down the Mississippi and starve the Gulf of Mexico of oxygen each summer.
reading: Corn needs nitrogen. Farmers supply it as fertilizer, and much of what they apply washes off fields in spring rains or drains through the buried tile pipes that keep fields dry. From Illinois ditches it flows to the Illinois River, then the Mississippi, then the Gulf of Mexico. There, every summer, the extra *nutrients* feed a bloom of algae. The algae die, sink and decay, and decay uses up oxygen. A patch of bottom water thousands of square kilometers in size becomes too low in oxygen for fish and shrimp to live. Scientists call it the dead zone, or *hypoxic zone*, and Illinois is one of its largest sources.

Nothing in the Gulf caused this. It is the sum of choices made in fields a thousand kilometers upstream, each one reasonable on its own. That is the signature of many environmental problems: the cost lands somewhere else, on someone else, later. Economists call this an *externality*. Measuring it is the first step: the size of the dead zone has been mapped every summer since the 1980s, and nutrient loads in the Mississippi are tracked by the U.S. Geological Survey.

Chicago has its own history of sending problems downstream. In the 1800s the city's sewage flowed into the Chicago River and out into Lake Michigan, its drinking water, and typhoid and cholera killed thousands. In 1900 engineers finished a canal that reversed the river, sending waste south toward the Illinois River instead. It saved lives in Chicago and fouled the river for towns downstream for decades, until treatment plants and the 1972 Clean Water Act cleaned it up. The fish have since come back.

Solutions to nutrient pollution work at the source. Applying fertilizer in the right amount at the right time, based on soil tests, cuts loss and saves money. Cover crops take up leftover nitrogen. Restored wetlands and buffer strips filter drainage water before it reaches a ditch. Illinois has a Nutrient Loss Reduction Strategy with numerical targets, and progress has been slow. The physics is clear; changing thousands of individual decisions is the hard part.

words.d: a substance living things need to grow, such as nitrogen or phosphorus
an area of water with so little oxygen that most animals cannot live there; also called a dead zone
a cost of an action that falls on people who did not take the action
water that flows off land into streams, carrying soil and chemicals with it

look.title: Following One Bag of Fertilizer
look.text: A farmer near Bloomington spreads nitrogen fertilizer on a cornfield in early April. Two days later, 4 centimeters of rain falls on the still-bare field. Water drains through tile pipes into a ditch, the ditch into the Sangamon River, the Sangamon into the Illinois, the Illinois into the Mississippi at Grafton. Three months later, shrimp boats off Louisiana pull up empty nets in a patch of dead water.
look.prompt: Trace the nitrogen's path and name each point where a different choice could have kept more of it in the field. Who pays the cost at the end, and who made the decisions?

check.q: What causes the Gulf of Mexico dead zone?
choices: Oil spills
Warm water from the Gulf Stream
Nutrients from upstream feeding algae whose decay uses up oxygen
Overfishing
check.why: Excess nitrogen and phosphorus trigger algae blooms. When the algae decay, bacteria consume the water's oxygen.

check.q: Why is the dead zone a good example of an externality?
choices: Because it happens outside the United States
Because it is caused by natural forces alone
Because it affects only the people who caused it
Because the cost falls on Gulf fishers far from the fields where the decisions were made
check.why: The people who bear the cost did not make the choices that caused it. That mismatch makes such problems hard to solve.

check.q: Why did Chicago reverse its river in 1900?
choices: To keep sewage out of Lake Michigan, the city's drinking water
To make the river flow faster for ships
To create a dead zone
To supply water to farms
check.why: Sewage in the lake caused deadly disease outbreaks. Reversing the river sent waste away from the water intake, though downstream towns paid for it.

lessons.title: The Air We Share
lessons.mainIdea: Pollution problems have been solved before when the science was clear and the substitutes existed; carbon dioxide is harder because it comes from nearly everything.
reading: In 1985 scientists reported a hole in the *ozone layer* over Antarctica. High in the atmosphere, ozone absorbs the sun's ultraviolet light, which causes skin cancer and damages crops. The culprit was a family of chemicals called CFCs, used in spray cans, refrigerators and foam. Their danger had been predicted in 1974 from lab chemistry, then confirmed by measurements over the pole. Within two years the world's nations signed the Montreal Protocol of 1987 to phase them out. Substitutes were available, and the ozone layer is now slowly healing.

Acid rain is another success. Sulfur from coal plants in the Midwest fell as acid across the Northeast, killing fish in lakes and weakening forests. The 1990 Clean Air Act amendments set a cap on sulfur emissions and let plants trade allowances, so cuts happened where they were cheapest. Sulfur emissions fell by far more than half at a fraction of the predicted cost, and many lakes have recovered. Chicago's air, thick with coal smoke in the 1950s, is far cleaner today for the same reason.

Carbon dioxide is harder for three reasons. It comes from nearly every engine, furnace, power plant and factory on Earth, not one product or one industry. It lasts in the air for centuries, so past emissions keep acting. And its effects land on everyone, including people and nations that emitted little, which makes agreement difficult. The science is as clear as it was for ozone; the substitutes are spreading fast but are not yet everywhere.

The scale of the challenge tracks the scale of humanity. The world's population reached 1 billion around 1800 and 8 billion in 2022, and energy use per person has grown even faster. Earth's systems now respond to human choices at a planetary level. That is a new situation in the planet's history, and it makes the next section's question, how to weigh solutions, a question every citizen will face.

words.d: a region of the upper atmosphere where ozone gas absorbs harmful ultraviolet light
chlorofluorocarbon, a chemical once used in sprays and refrigerators that destroys ozone
rain made acidic by sulfur and nitrogen pollution from burning fuel
a rule that limits total pollution and lets companies buy and sell shares of the limit

look.title: World Population Milestones
look.prompt: How long did each added billion take? What does this pattern imply about the demands on water, soil, energy and air in your lifetime compared with your great-grandparents'?

check.q: Why did the Montreal Protocol succeed quickly?
choices: The science was clear and substitutes for CFCs already existed
CFCs were only used in one country
Ozone repaired itself without help
Spray cans were banned worldwide in 1974
check.why: Clear evidence plus available replacements made the phase-out cheap enough that nations agreed within two years.

check.q: How did the 1990 acid rain program cut sulfur cheaply?
choices: By shutting every coal plant
By capping total emissions and letting plants trade allowances so cuts happened where cheapest
By switching all plants to nuclear
By moving plants to the Northeast
check.why: A cap set the total; trading found the lowest-cost reductions. Emissions fell far more than half at a fraction of the predicted cost.

check.q: Which reason makes carbon dioxide harder to control than CFCs?
choices: Carbon dioxide is not a greenhouse gas
Carbon dioxide is invisible
It comes from nearly every fuel-burning activity and lingers for centuries
Nobody has measured it
check.why: CFCs came from a few products with ready substitutes. Carbon dioxide comes from almost all energy use, and past emissions keep acting.

lessons.title: Cost, Benefit and Constraint
lessons.mainIdea: Engineers judge a solution by its benefits, its costs and the constraints it must satisfy, and no real solution wins on every count.
reading: A coastal town faces rising seas and stronger storms. It could build a seawall, restore a marsh that absorbs waves, raise its buildings, or move back from the shore. Each choice protects something and gives something up. Choosing well takes a method, and the method is the same whether the problem is a seawall, a power plant or a school lunch program: name the *criteria*, name the *constraints*, estimate the costs and benefits of each option, and compare.

Criteria are what a good solution must do: keep people safe, keep costs down, keep the beach, keep the fishery. Constraints are hard limits: the budget, the law, the physics, the time. A seawall may score highest on safety but fail the budget and destroy the beach. Marsh restoration is cheaper and improves fishing but takes years to grow and cannot stop the biggest storms. A *trade-off* is what you accept losing on one criterion to gain on another.

Costs and benefits are rarely on the same scale. A seawall's cost is in dollars; the lost beach is in summer afternoons and tourist jobs; safety is in lives. Some benefits come now and some in thirty years. Some costs fall on the town and some, like the marsh's loss, fall on fish and on people not yet born. Honest analysis puts all of these on the table, says which are measured and which are estimated, and does not hide the ones that are hard to count.

Scientists supply the numbers: how high the water will get, how strong the wall must be, how fast a marsh grows. They do not get to decide whose beach matters more. That belongs to the people who live with the result. The best decisions come when the science is laid out clearly and the community, understanding it, chooses. That is why science literacy is a civic skill and not just a school subject.

words.d: the goals a good solution must meet, used to compare options
a hard limit a solution cannot break, such as a budget, a law or the laws of physics
giving up some of one thing you want to gain more of another
comparing what a choice costs against what it gains, including costs that are hard to count

look.title: The Levee Vote
look.text: A river town of 3,000 people must decide. Option one: raise the levee for 40 million dollars, protecting the downtown against a hundred-year flood but not a larger one. Option two: buy out the 60 homes on the floodplain for 15 million dollars, turn the land into a park, and let the river spread. Option three: do nothing and hope. The town's whole yearly budget is 12 million dollars, and federal aid will cover half of either project.
look.prompt: List the criteria and the constraints. Which option would you argue for, what does it give up, and who bears each cost?

check.q: Which of these is a constraint rather than a criterion?
choices: The solution should preserve the beach
The solution should protect lives
The solution should be attractive
The solution must cost no more than 20 million dollars
check.why: A constraint is a hard limit that cannot be broken. The others are goals to weigh against each other.

check.q: What is a trade-off?
choices: Accepting less of one goal to gain more of another
A solution that satisfies every criterion
A cost that falls on another town
A rule that cannot be broken
check.why: Real solutions rarely win on every count. Choosing means deciding which losses are acceptable for which gains.

check.q: Why can scientists not settle by themselves whether a town should build a seawall?
choices: Scientists do not understand seawalls
The choice depends on values, such as whose beach and whose safety matter more
Seawalls are always the right answer
The physics is unknown
check.why: Science gives the numbers: water height, wall strength, marsh growth. Weighing lives, jobs and beaches against each other is a community decision.

lessons.title: Mitigation and Adaptation
lessons.mainIdea: Mitigation reduces the cause of a change; adaptation reduces its harm; a sensible plan does both.
reading: Two words organize the response to climate change. *Mitigation* means reducing the cause: emitting less greenhouse gas, or pulling it back out of the air. *Adaptation* means preparing for the changes that are already coming: bigger storm drains, heat plans, drought-tolerant crops, moved homes. Mitigation is like fixing the leak; adaptation is like mopping the floor and moving the furniture. Since some warming is already locked in by past emissions, both are needed.

Mitigation options are known and the argument is about pace and cost. Replacing coal and gas plants with wind, solar, nuclear and storage cuts emissions at the source. Electric vehicles, better insulation and efficient motors cut the energy needed in the first place. Forests and soils can store carbon. Machines that capture carbon dioxide from smokestacks or the air exist but are costly and small so far. Each option has a price per ton avoided, and the cheapest ones, efficiency and wind, are already spreading on cost alone.

Adaptation in Illinois looks practical. The federal National Climate Assessment reports that the Midwest is seeing more heavy downpours, warmer winters, and more days of heat stress for crops and people. So Chicago is expanding the Deep Tunnel, planting trees against the heat island, and mapping which neighborhoods are most vulnerable. Farmers are shifting planting dates and drainage. Engineers now design culverts and sewers for the rainfall of the coming decades, not the records of the last century.

The two strategies interact. Every ton of mitigation reduces the adaptation the future will need; every dollar of adaptation buys time for mitigation to work. Doing only adaptation means running faster and faster to stay in place. Doing only mitigation ignores the flood already at the door. The evidence supports doing both, weighing each action with the criteria and constraints of the last lesson.

words.d: actions that reduce the cause of a problem, such as cutting greenhouse gas emissions
actions that reduce the harm from a change that is already happening or expected
technology that removes carbon dioxide from smokestacks or the air and stores it
the ability of a community or system to absorb a shock and recover

look.title: The National Climate Assessment on the Midwest
look.text: The Fourth National Climate Assessment, prepared by federal agencies and released in 2018, reported that the Midwest is experiencing more frequent heavy rainfall events and warmer, wetter springs that delay planting and increase soil erosion and nutrient runoff, and that rising summer heat and humidity are expected to reduce yields of major crops and increase health risks in cities unless communities adapt.
look.cite: U.S. Global Change Research Program, Fourth National Climate Assessment, Volume II, 2018
look.prompt: Pick one Midwest impact the report names and propose one mitigation action and one adaptation action that address it. Which is local and which is global?

check.q: Which is an example of adaptation?
choices: Replacing a coal plant with wind turbines
Building larger storm sewers for heavier rainfall
Driving an electric car
Planting a forest to store carbon
check.why: Adaptation reduces harm from changes already coming. Bigger sewers do not cut emissions; they handle the bigger rains.

check.q: Why are both mitigation and adaptation needed?
choices: Because mitigation has failed
Because adaptation is cheaper
Because some change is already locked in, while further change can still be reduced
Because they are the same thing
check.why: Past emissions guarantee some warming, so adaptation is needed. Future emissions are still a choice, so mitigation matters.

check.q: Which mitigation options are spreading fastest on cost alone?
choices: Carbon capture machines
Coal plants
Nuclear plants
Efficiency and wind power
check.why: Efficiency and wind now cost less per unit than many fossil options, so they grow without needing subsidies.

lessons.title: Illinois in Fifty Years
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois's food, water and energy futures are linked, and choices made in fields, cities and statehouses now will shape all three.
reading: Picture central Illinois in 2075. What will be on the land? The safest answer is still corn and soybeans, but the details are open. Some fields may carry solar panels high enough to farm beneath, an approach called *agrivoltaics* that is being tested in the state now. Wind turbines will likely be taller and fewer. Prairie strips and wetlands may thread between fields, holding soil and filtering water. Or the land may look much as it does now, with soil a little thinner and ditches a little browner. Both futures follow from choices.

Water ties it together. Wetter springs and hotter summers mean more runoff when fields are bare and more thirst when crops need water. Farmers who build soil with cover crops and no-till gain a sponge: soil rich in organic matter holds far more water per meter than depleted soil. That same practice keeps nitrogen out of the Gulf and stores carbon. One change addresses four problems, which is the mark of a strong solution.

Energy is the fastest-moving piece. Illinois already has a low-carbon backbone in its nuclear plants and a growing wind and solar fleet. The open questions are the ones engineers weigh with criteria and constraints: how much storage, how many transmission lines, whether to keep aging reactors running, how to help coal communities. Each answer is a trade-off among cost, reliability, land and jobs.

None of this is decided by nature. Earth's systems set the constraints: the rain, the soil, the sun, the physics of carbon dioxide. Within them, the outcome is human. The Dust Bowl ended not because the wind quit but because people changed how they farmed, using evidence gathered by scientists and rules made by citizens. That is the whole lesson of this unit, compressed: understand the system, measure honestly, weigh the trade-offs, and choose.

words.d: placing solar panels over farmland so crops or grazing continue beneath them
decayed plant and animal material in soil that holds water and nutrients
a high-voltage power line that carries electricity long distances from plants to cities

look.title: Two Fields in a Wet Spring
look.text: Neighboring fields near Champaign get 6 centimeters of rain in one April night. Field A was left bare after harvest and plowed. Its ditch runs brown by morning, and puddles stand in the low spots for days. Field B was planted to rye last fall and will be planted through the rye stubble without plowing. Its ditch runs nearly clear, and the soil is damp but firm by noon.
look.prompt: Explain what happened to the water and the soil in each field, and list every downstream benefit of Field B's choice, from the ditch to the Gulf to the atmosphere.

check.q: Why does soil rich in organic matter help with both drought and flooding?
choices: It holds more water, soaking up heavy rain and releasing it slowly in dry spells
It repels water entirely
It is heavier and cannot wash away
It needs no fertilizer
check.why: Organic matter acts like a sponge, absorbing rain instead of shedding it and keeping moisture available for crops later.

check.q: What is agrivoltaics?
choices: Growing corn to make fuel
Solar panels placed over farmland so crops or grazing continue beneath
Using tractors powered by electricity
Wind turbines on a farm
check.why: Agrivoltaics combines solar energy and agriculture on the same land, one way to reduce the land trade-off of solar power.

check.q: What ended the Dust Bowl's worst damage?
choices: The wind stopped blowing forever
The soil grew back on its own
People changed farming practices based on evidence, plus the return of rain
Farmers moved to Illinois
check.why: Rain returned in 1939, but contour plowing, windbreaks and cover held the soil through later droughts. Choices changed the outcome.

review.q: What made the Dust Bowl more than a natural disaster?
choices: Drought struck land that had been stripped of its grass cover by plowing
The wind was stronger than ever before
The soil was naturally sandy
Farmers had planted too many trees
review.why: Drought is natural. Bare, plowed soil with no roots to hold it was a human choice, and changing the choice changed the outcome.

review.q: Which is a nonrenewable resource?
choices: Wind
Coal
Sunlight
A forest cut slower than it regrows
review.why: Coal formed over hundreds of millions of years and will not be replaced on any human timescale.

review.q: A town moves its houses off the floodplain. Which part of risk did it reduce?
choices: The hazard
The rainfall
The exposure
The river's height
review.why: The flood still comes. Removing people and buildings from its path reduces exposure, the part people control most.

review.q: What causes the dead zone in the Gulf of Mexico?
choices: Cold water
Hurricanes
Overfishing by shrimp boats
Nutrients from upstream farms feeding algae whose decay uses up oxygen
review.why: Nitrogen and phosphorus from the Mississippi basin, including Illinois, fuel algae blooms that strip oxygen from bottom water.

review.q: Why did the Montreal Protocol work faster than efforts to cut carbon dioxide?
choices: CFCs came from a few products with ready substitutes, while carbon dioxide comes from nearly all energy use
Ozone was more important than climate
CFCs were already illegal
Carbon dioxide had not been measured yet
review.why: A narrow source and available replacements made the CFC phase-out cheap. Carbon dioxide has neither advantage.

review.q: Which statement about nuclear power in Illinois is accurate?
choices: It supplies almost none of the state's electricity
It supplies roughly half of the state's electricity and emits no carbon dioxide while running
It is the state's main source of air pollution
It has been fully replaced by coal
review.why: Illinois has more reactors than any other state, and they produce about half its electricity without carbon emissions, though waste and cost remain trade-offs.

review.q: Building bigger storm sewers for heavier rains is an example of:
choices: Mitigation
An externality
Adaptation
Recharge
review.why: It does not reduce the cause of climate change. It reduces the harm from a change already arriving, which is adaptation.

review.q: Which of these is a constraint in a decision about a levee?
choices: Protecting the downtown
Keeping the river view
Reducing insurance costs
A budget that cannot exceed 12 million dollars
review.why: A budget ceiling is a hard limit. The others are criteria to be weighed against one another.
